original_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
reformulated_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller parts, until they can be absorbed and absorbed into the body.
rationale: "assimilated" was replaced with "absorbed", producing the redundant "absorbed and absorbed" instead of two distinct processes (absorption then assimilation); overall meaning is still roughly conveyed but the duplication is confusing.

original_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
reformulated_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into least and finer components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
rationale: "smaller and smaller" became "least and finer" — "least" does not mean progressively smaller and does not parallel "finer", producing a semantically confusing phrase.

original_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
reformulated_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and absorbed into the body.
rationale: Same as the core-word variant: "assimilated" -> "absorbed" creates the redundant "absorbed and absorbed", losing the distinction between the two named processes.

original_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
reformulated_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and absorbed into the body.
rationale: Identical defect to the other single-word-change variants: "assimilated" replaced by "absorbed", yielding the redundant "absorbed and absorbed".

original_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
reformulated_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into least and finer components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
rationale: Same "least and finer" substitution for "smaller and smaller" seen in the sparse_common_sound variant — semantically wrong and confusing.

original_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
reformulated_text: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into least and finer components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
rationale: Same "least and finer" substitution for "smaller and smaller" — "least" does not function as a valid parallel comparative here.

original_text: Chewing mixes the food with saliva to produce a food bolus to be swallowed down the esophagus to enter the stomach.
reformulated_text: Chewing mixes the food with saliva to create a food bolus to swallow down the esophageal to enter the stomach.

changes.original: Chewing mixes the food with saliva to produce a food bolus to be swallowed down the esophagus to enter the stomach.
changes.replacement: Chewing mixes the food with saliva to create a food bolus to swallow down the esophageal to enter the stomach.

rationale: "esophagus" (noun) was replaced with "esophageal" (adjective only), leaving "swallow down the esophageal to enter the stomach" without a noun — ungrammatical and confusing to parse.

original_text: Peristalsis is the rhythmic contraction of muscles that begins in the esophagus and continues along the wall of the stomach and the rest of the gastrointestinal tract.
reformulated_text: Peristalaxis is the rhythmic contracting of muscles that begins in the esophagum and continues along the wall of the stomach and the rest of the intestines.

changes.original: Peristalsis is the rhythmic contraction of muscles that begins in the esophagus and continues along the wall of the stomach and the rest of the gastrointestinal tract.
changes.replacement: Peristalaxis is the rhythmic contracting of muscles that begins in the esophagum and continues along the wall of the stomach and the rest of the intestines.

rationale: "Peristalsis" and "esophagus" were turned into non-existent words ("Peristalaxis", "esophagum"), and "gastrointestinal tract" was narrowed to "intestines", excluding the esophagus/stomach the original term covered.

original_text: Most of the digestion of food takes place in the small intestine.
reformulated_text: Most of the digestion of food takes place in the little intestine.
rationale: "small intestine" is a fixed anatomical term; "little intestine" is not standard terminology, though the organ referred to remains clear.

original_text: Water and some minerals are reabsorbed back into the blood in the large intestine.
reformulated_text: Water and some minerals are assumed back into the blood in the large intestine.
rationale: "reabsorbed" was replaced with "assumed", an unrelated word (meaning presumed) — "assumed back into the blood" is nonsensical.

original_text: Bile acts partly as a surfactant which lowers the surface tension between either two liquids or a solid and a liquid and helps to emulsify the fats in the chyme.
reformulated_text: Bile acts partly as a lubricant which lowers the surface pressure between either two solids or a solid and a liquid and helps to emollidate the fats in the chyme.

changes.original: Bile acts partly as a surfactant which lowers the surface tension between either two liquids or a solid and a liquid and helps to emulsify the fats in the chyme.
changes.replacement: Bile acts partly as a lubricant which lowers the surface pressure between either two solids or a solid and a liquid and helps to emollidate the fats in the chyme.

rationale: "two liquids" was changed to "two solids", reversing the physical claim (surfactants act between liquid interfaces, not solid-solid ones); additionally "surfactant"->"lubricant" and "surface tension"->"surface pressure" are wrong technical substitutions, and "emulsify"->"emollidate" is an invented word.

original_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
reformulated_text: Nutrition is the chemical and physical process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
rationale: "physiological" (organism-function specific) was flattened to "physical" (generic), losing precision, though the overall definition of nutrition still basically holds.

original_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
reformulated_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to give its life.
rationale: "support its life" became "give its life", which idiomatically means to sacrifice/lose one's life — nearly the opposite of sustaining life.

original_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
reformulated_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physical process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
rationale: Same "physiological"->"physical" precision loss as the core-word variant.

original_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
reformulated_text: The nutritional process is the biological and physiochemical process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.

changes.original: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
changes.replacement: The nutritional process is the biological and physiochemical process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.

rationale: Restructured to "The nutritional process is the ... process by which...", a circular/redundant construction ("process is...process"), and "biochemical and physiological" was reordered to "biological and physiochemical" — awkward but meaning is still roughly recoverable.

original_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
reformulated_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physical act by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
rationale: "physiological process" became "physical act" — "act" implies a single action rather than an ongoing biological process, and "physical" again loses the biology-specific sense of "physiological".

original_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
reformulated_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to give its life.
rationale: Same as the dense_mixed_generic variant: "support its life" -> "give its life", idiomatically inverting the intended meaning of sustaining life.

original_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
reformulated_text: Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to give its life.
rationale: Same "support its life" -> "give its life" substitution, which idiomatically suggests sacrificing life rather than sustaining it.

original_text: Over-nutrition of micronutrient is a major cause of obesity and increases the risk of developing various non-communicable diseases ( NCDs ), including type 2 diabetes, stroke, hypertension, coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, and some forms of cancer.
reformulated_text: Over-nutrition of micronutrient is a major cause of obesity and increases the chance of developing various non-communicable diseases ( NCDs ), including type 2 diabetes, shot, hypertension, coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, and some forms of cancer.
rationale: "stroke" was replaced with "shot", an unrelated word that does not belong in a list of diseases, producing a nonsensical item in the disease list.

original_text: All forms of life require carbon, energy, and water as well as various other molecules.
reformulated_text: All forms of life require carbon, energy, and water as well as various other compounds.
rationale: "molecules" was narrowed to "compounds" (compounds are a subset of molecules requiring two or more distinct elements), a minor taxonomic narrowing of the claim.

original_text: Animals require complex nutrients such as carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, obtaining them by consuming other organisms.
reformulated_text: Animals require complex nutrients such as sugars, lipids, and proteins, obtaining them by consuming other beings.
rationale: "carbohydrates" was narrowed to "sugars" (sugars are only one subtype of carbohydrate, alongside starches and fiber), narrowing the scientific claim; "organisms"->"beings" is an acceptable synonym.

original_text: Nutrients are absorbed by the cells and used in metabolic biochemical reactions.
reformulated_text: Nutritions are absorbed by the cells and used in metabolic biological reactions.
rationale: "Nutrients" was changed to "Nutritions" — "nutrition" is an uncountable/abstract noun and pluralizing it this way is ungrammatical; "biochemical"->"biological" also loses precision.

original_text: Nutrients are absorbed by the cells and used in metabolic biochemical reactions.
reformulated_text: Nutrients are absorbed by the cases and used in metabolic biochemical reactions.
rationale: "cells" was replaced with "cases", an unrelated word that makes "absorbed by the cases" nonsensical in this biological context.

original_text: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are rearranged and the reaction is accompanied by an energy change as new products are generated.
reformulated_text: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are arranged and the reaction is followed by an energy change as new products are generated.
rationale: "rearranged" was shortened to "arranged", dropping the "re-" that conveys atoms being reconfigured from an existing state, a subtle but real meaning shift; "accompanied by"->"followed by" also shifts simultaneity to sequence.

original_text: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are rearranged and the reaction is accompanied by an energy change as new products are generated.
reformulated_text: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are rearranged and the reaction is followed by an energy change as new products are generated.
rationale: "accompanied by" (simultaneous) became "followed by" (sequential/after), a subtle shift in the temporal relationship between the reaction and the energy change.

original_text: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are rearranged and the reaction is accompanied by an energy change as new products are generated.
reformulated_text: When chemical reaction occur, the atoms are arranged and the reaction is followed by an energy change as new products are generated.

changes.original: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are rearranged and the reaction is accompanied by an energy change as new products are generated.
changes.replacement: When chemical reaction occur, the atoms are arranged and the reaction is followed by an energy change as new products are generated.

rationale: "chemical reactions occur" became "chemical reaction occur" — singular subject with plural verb, a clear subject-verb agreement error; it also carries the "arranged"/"followed by" precision losses seen in other variants.

original_text: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are rearranged and the reaction is accompanied by an energy change as new products are generated.
reformulated_text: When chemical reactions occur, the atoms are rearranged and the reaction is followed by an energy change as new chemicals are generated.
rationale: Same "accompanied by"->"followed by" temporal-nuance shift; "products"->"chemicals" is an acceptable loose synonym.

original_text: Chemical reactions are usually characterized by a chemical change, and they yield one or more products, which usually have properties different from the reactants.
reformulated_text: Chemical reactions are usually characterised by a chemical change and they yield one or more products, which usually have different characteristics from the reactionants.

changes.original: Chemical reactions are usually characterized by a chemical change, and they yield one or more products, which usually have properties different from the reactants.
changes.replacement: Chemical reactions are usually characterised by a chemical change and they yield one or more products, which usually have different characteristics from the reactionants.

rationale: "reactants" was corrupted into "reactionants", a non-existent word; the intended term is still inferable from context but is not valid English.

original_text: Chemical reactions are usually characterized by a chemical change, and they yield one or more products, which usually have properties different from the reactants.
reformulated_text: Chemical answers are usually characterized by a chemical change, and they yield one or more products, which usually have properties different from the chemicals.
rationale: "Chemical reactions" became "Chemical answers" — "answers" is an unrelated word, making the sentence's subject nonsensical.

original_text: Typically, reaction rates increase with increasing temperature because there is more thermal energy available to reach the activation energy necessary for breaking bonds between atoms.
reformulated_text: Usually, reaction rates increase with rising temperatures because there is more thermal energy available to reach the activated energy necessary for breaking bonds between atoms.

changes.original: Typically, reaction rates increase with increasing temperature because there is more thermal energy available to reach the activation energy necessary for breaking bonds between atoms.
changes.replacement: Usually, reaction rates increase with rising temperatures because there is more thermal energy available to reach the activated energy necessary for breaking bonds between atoms.

rationale: The fixed term "activation energy" was changed to "activated energy", a non-standard variant of the technical term, though the overall meaning is still recoverable.

original_text: In a bimolecular reaction, two molecules collide and react with each other.
reformulated_text: Two molecules collide and react with each other in a bimolécular reaction.

changes.original: In a bimolecular reaction, two molecules collide and react with each other.
changes.replacement: Two molecules collide and react with each other in a bimolécular reaction.

rationale: "bimolecular" was rendered with an accent as "bimolécular", an incorrect spelling of the technical term; the restructuring of the sentence itself is fine and meaning-preserving.

original_text: The forward and reverse reactions are competing with each other and differ in reaction rates.
reformulated_text: The forward and reverse results are rivaling with each other and differ in reaction rates.
rationale: "reactions" was replaced with "results", removing the core chemistry concept (forward/reverse reactions) and leaving an incoherent claim that "results...differ in reaction rates".

original_text: A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, unless it is acted upon by a force.
reformulated_text: A body stays at rest or in motion at a steady speed in a line unless it is acted upon by a force.

changes.original: A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, unless it is acted upon by a force.
changes.replacement: A body stays at rest or in motion at a steady speed in a line unless it is acted upon by a force.

rationale: "straight line" was shortened to just "line", dropping a qualifier essential to Newton's first law (constant-speed motion along a curved line still involves acceleration), weakening the physical accuracy of the stated law.

original_text: A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, unless it is acted upon by a force.
reformulated_text: A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant rate in a right line, unless it is acted upon by a force.
rationale: "straight line" became "right line", an archaic term for straight line that a modern listener is likely to misread as "correct line" or a directional "right" line, creating ambiguity despite technically being an old synonym.

original_text: At any instant of time, the net force on a body is equal to the body's acceleration multiplied by its mass or, equivalently, the rate at which the body's momentum is changing with time.
reformulated_text: At any instant of time, the net force on a body is equal to the body's accelerated mass or the rate at which the movement of the body is changing with time.

changes.original: At any instant of time, the net force on a body is equal to the body's acceleration multiplied by its mass or, equivalently, the rate at which the body's momentum is changing with time.
changes.replacement: At any instant of time, the net force on a body is equal to the body's accelerated mass or the rate at which the movement of the body is changing with time.

rationale: "acceleration multiplied by its mass" became "accelerated mass", turning the product of two distinct quantities (F=ma) into a garbled single compound; separately, "momentum" was replaced by the vague "movement", dropping the specific physical quantity the rate-of-change definition depends on.

original_text: At any instant of time, the net force on a body is equal to the body's acceleration multiplied by its mass or, equivalently, the rate at which the body's momentum is changing with time.
reformulated_text: At any instant of time, the net force on a body is equal to the body's acceleration multiplied by its mass or, equivalently, the value at which the body's momentum is changing with time.
rationale: "the rate at which...is changing" became "the value at which...is changing" — "rate" (a change-per-time concept) is not equivalent to "value", making the statement imprecise though still roughly interpretable.

original_text: If two bodies exert forces on each other, these forces have the same magnitude but opposite directions.
reformulated_text: If two bodies exert forces on each other, these forces have the one magnitude but opposite directions.
rationale: "same magnitude" became "one magnitude", an unusual dialectal phrasing ("the one X" = "the same X") likely to read as confusing or ungrammatical to a general audience, even though the intended meaning is recoverable.

original_text: Newton's first law expresses the principle of inertia: the natural behavior of a body is to move in a straight line at constant speed.
reformulated_text: Newton's first law expresses the principle of inertia: the natural behavior of a body is to move in a true line at constant velocity.
rationale: "straight line" became "true line", a non-standard substitution that risks being read as "accurate/real line" rather than "straight"; "speed"->"velocity" is redundant with the line description but not itself a factual error.

original_text: When the net force on a body is equal to zero, then by Newton's second law, the body do not accelerate, and it is said to be in mechanical equilibrium.
reformulated_text: When the net force on a body is equal to zero, then by Newton's second law the body does not accelerated, and it is said to be in a physical balance.

changes.original: When the net force on a body is equal to zero, then by Newton's second law, the body do not accelerate, and it is said to be in mechanical equilibrium.
changes.replacement: When the net force on a body is equal to zero, then by Newton's second law the body does not accelerated, and it is said to be in a physical balance.

rationale: "does not accelerated" is an ungrammatical verb form (should be "accelerate"); additionally the fixed term "mechanical equilibrium" was replaced with the vaguer "physical balance".

original_text: In other words, if one body exerts a force on a second body, the second body is also exerting a force on the first body, of equal magnitude in the opposite direction.
reformulated_text: In other words, if a body exerts a force on a second body, the second body also exerts force on the first body of equal force in the opposing directions.

changes.original: In other words, if one body exerts a force on a second body, the second body is also exerting a force on the first body, of equal magnitude in the opposite direction.
changes.replacement: In other words, if a body exerts a force on a second body, the second body also exerts force on the first body of equal force in the opposing directions.

rationale: "of equal magnitude" became "of equal force", creating a circular/redundant phrase ("exerts force...of equal force") that is awkward though the intended meaning (equal-sized opposing forces) still comes through.

original_text: A star is a luminous spheroid of plasma held together by self-gravity.
reformulated_text: A star is a luminous spheroid of plasma, which is surrounded by self gravity.

changes.original: A star is a luminous spheroid of plasma held together by self-gravity.
changes.replacement: A star is a luminous spheroid of plasma, which is surrounded by self gravity.

rationale: "held together by self-gravity" (gravity as an internal cohesive force) became "surrounded by self gravity" (gravity as an external envelope), reversing the physical relationship between the star's matter and its own gravity.

original_text: A star is a luminous spheroid of plasma held together by self-gravity.
reformulated_text: A star is a luminous sphéroid of plasma, surrounded by self-gravitational gravity.

changes.original: A star is a luminous spheroid of plasma held together by self-gravity.

original_text: A star shines for most of its active life due to the thermonuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core.
reformulated_text: A star glows in its core for most of its activity life due to the thermonuklear fusion of helium in it.

changes.original: A star shines for most of its active life due to the thermonuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core.
changes.replacement: A star glows in its core for most of its activity life due to the thermonuklear fusion of helium in it.

rationale: Drops 'of hydrogen into' so 'fusion of hydrogen into helium' becomes just 'fusion of helium', changing the described nuclear process from hydrogen-to-helium conversion to helium fusion; also contains 'activity life' and the typo 'thermonuklear'.

original_text: This process releases energy that traverses the star's interior and radiates into outer space.
reformulated_text: This process releases energy that passes through the star's inner space and radiate into outer space.

changes.original: This process releases energy that traverses the star's interior and radiates into outer space.
